s: Chapter Five: Context Management and Reliability
Chapter five.
Let's open with a story.
Picture a refund agent.
It's forty-five turns into a chat with an unhappy customer.
Early on, the customer said the order cost one hundred and fifty-nine dollars and ninety-nine cents.
The order system said one hundred and forty-nine ninety-nine.
And the refund window stood at day twenty-eight of thirty.
Then the conversation got long.
The system tidied up its own memory twice, the way it was designed to.
And somewhere around turn forty, the agent asked the customer for the amount again.
Then it quoted the wrong figure back.
Nobody changed the model.
Nothing crashed.
No error appeared in any log.
The system simply forgot the one number that mattered.
And it forgot it politely.
That is this chapter in one story.
Domain five of the Claude Certified Architect, Foundations exam is called Context Management and Reliability.
It carries fifteen percent of the exam weight.
That's roughly nine questions on a sixty-question paper.
It has six task statements.
We'll take them in order, one part each.
First.
Keeping critical information alive through long conversations.
Second.
Deciding when a system should stop and fetch a human, and what it should do when a request is unclear.
Third.
How failures travel between agents without turning into false good news.
Fourth.
Exploring a large codebase without drowning the model in it.
Fifth.
Human review, and whether a model's confidence number means anything.
And sixth.
Keeping track of where every claim came from when several sources are combined.
Here's the thread that runs through all six.
The exam keeps showing you failures that look identical from the outside.
An agent that contradicts itself.
An answer that is confidently wrong.
A review queue nobody trusts.
They all present as "the system is unreliable."
But each has a different cause and a different fix.
And the fixes are not interchangeable.
The tempting wrong answer is almost always a global remedy.
A bigger memory.
A retry.
A higher threshold.
More sources.
Those make a symptom rarer, without touching its cause.
The second recurring axis is cost.
Often two answers both work.
The credited one buys the same reliability with fewer tokens, fewer hours of human review, or fewer round trips to the customer.
Keep those two ideas in your pocket for the whole chapter.
One, find the actual cause.
Two, watch the cost.
Coming up in part one: keeping critical information alive in long conversations.
And yes, we'll come back to that refund agent.
